properties.value: The model named in the body is served unchanged unless an operator-declared rewrite rule matches its name, in which case one target is drawn at random in proportion to declared integer weights and written back into the body.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees the served model is either the requested one or a declared rewrite target; refuses any quality- or price-based substitution, and with equal weights (or a total weight of zero) the draw is uniform and not reproducible.

properties.value: Every candidate endpoint passes a filter chain, then accumulates a weighted sum of scorer outputs each clamped into the unit interval, and the picker returns the highest-scoring endpoint with random tie-breaking.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees exactly one endpoint by default, drawn from the surviving candidates; refuses to guarantee determinism, because ties are broken by a wall-clock-seeded shuffle. Shipped weights: queue depth 2.0, memory pressure 2.0, prefix locality 3.0, unweighted scorers 1.0.

properties.value: prefix locality carries half again the pull of queue depth or memory pressure in the shipped weights
properties.tradeoff: large throughput win from cache reuse, at the risk of piling repeat traffic onto an already busy endpoint

properties.value: each signal contributes at most its own weight because every score is clamped into the unit interval before weighting
properties.tradeoff: a misbehaving signal cannot hijack the decision, but a genuinely extreme signal is flattened to the same value as a merely bad one

properties.value: Admission is decided BEFORE endpoints are located. The legacy controller refuses a request only if its priority is negative and mean pool saturation is at least 1.0; the flow-control controller instead blocks the caller in a per-workload bounded queue and returns a typed outcome.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees that a request with non-negative priority is never refused for load on the legacy path, and that every queued request ends in exactly one terminal outcome visible to the caller: dispatched, capacity-rejected (429), deadline-expired (503) or client-cancelled (503). Saturation is the mean over candidates of max(waiting/5, memory/0.8); a stale or metric-less endpoint contributes a full 1.0. Per-band queue capacity is 1 GB; the global byte and request caps default to unlimited, and the documented 5000-request per-band cap is never applied.

properties.value: an endpoint whose telemetry has gone quiet is treated as completely saturated when deciding whether to refuse
properties.tradeoff: fails safe against routing into a blind spot, but a telemetry outage alone can trigger refusals

properties.property: admission decided before targets are known
properties.value: the wait-or-refuse decision happens before the router works out which endpoints could serve the request
properties.tradeoff: keeps queueing ahead of all scheduling cost, but the decision cannot use request-specific candidate information

properties.value: every queued request is finalised exactly once and the caller always learns which of dispatched, capacity-rejected, deadline-expired or cancelled happened
properties.tradeoff: requests are never silently lost, at the cost of an intricate ownership protocol and a periodic sweeper

properties.value: not decided: there is no request or token quota accounting of any kind. The only headroom signal is live endpoint utilisation, converted into a dispatch ceiling per priority band.
properties.tradeoff: Refuses to guarantee anything about an upstream's published allowance. The nearest analogue is a per-endpoint ideal-capacity figure and a static usage ceiling that defaults to 1.0, meaning dispatch stops only at complete saturation, leaving no reserve.

properties.value: not decided at the request level. A scheduling or admission failure is returned to the caller immediately; there is no second attempt, no fallback endpoint and no back-off schedule anywhere.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees a single placement attempt per request and an explicit typed error on failure; refuses any retry or fallback, with the source carrying an open note acknowledging the gap. The only loop in the system re-places a request whose chosen shard began draining, after a short randomised pause.

properties.value: Endpoint health is inferred purely from telemetry freshness. The candidate set is every pod in the datastore; no error counting, quarantine or timed re-probe exists.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees that an endpoint whose state is older than 200 ms is scored as fully saturated and dropped from routing; refuses to guarantee exclusion when EVERY endpoint is stale, because the filter then returns the unfiltered list and knowingly routes into the dark. State refreshes every 50 ms; a separate 2 s staleness flag affects only the metric logger, not placement.

properties.value: if the freshness check would eliminate every endpoint, the unfiltered list is used instead
properties.tradeoff: keeps serving during a fleet-wide telemetry outage at the cost of knowingly sending traffic into the dark; note the per-profile filter chain does the opposite and fails closed

properties.value: there is no probe, cooldown or re-admission step, because nothing was ever taken out of rotation
properties.tradeoff: no state to get wrong and no flapping, but no protection against a persistently failing target

properties.value: Each request carries one integer priority from its workload objective (default 0, negative means expendable). Priority bands are dispatched strictly highest-first; within a workload the ordering policy decides, defaulting to arrival order, with an optional deadline ordering keyed on the request's declared time-to-first-token budget.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees strict priority-band ordering and head-of-line blocking: if the selected band is saturated the whole dispatch cycle stops rather than letting lower-priority work proceed. Under the deadline policy a request with no or malformed declared budget is assigned a far-future deadline and sorts last. A request's remaining deadline becomes its queue time to live, whose default is 0 meaning no limit, swept every 1 s.

properties.value: the sign of the priority, not its magnitude, decides whether the request may be discarded under load
properties.tradeoff: one crisp system-wide rule, but a cliff edge between one priority level and the next, and a fleet of all-default traffic has no valve at all

properties.value: if the most important pending work cannot be served right now, nothing less important is served either
properties.tradeoff: eliminates priority inversion, at the cost of idling capacity that lower-priority work could have used

properties.property: the deadline is also the patience
properties.value: how long a request waits in the queue is taken from its own remaining deadline, and with none it waits until the caller gives up
properties.tradeoff: no arbitrary cap to tune, but an unbounded default wait when the caller sets no deadline

properties.value: Work is partitioned into flows keyed by caller identity and priority; each flow gets its own queue inside its priority band, and a fairness policy chooses which flow's queue to serve next.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees only a shared byte budget per band (1 GB) and load spreading across shards by shortest-queue-by-bytes; refuses starvation-freedom by default, because the SHIPPED fairness policy ignores flow boundaries entirely and always takes the globally best pending item, so one workload can monopolise a band. Starvation-freedom requires explicitly selecting the rotating policy. Idle flows are reclaimed after 5 minutes, bands after 10.

properties.value: guaranteed turn-taking between workloads exists but must be switched on deliberately; the shipped policy takes whichever pending request ranks best overall
properties.tradeoff: the default gives globally optimal ordering and no bookkeeping, but one heavy workload can hold the line indefinitely

properties.property: load spread by backlog, not by hash
properties.value: an arriving request joins whichever parallel worker currently holds the least of that workload's backlog
properties.tradeoff: balances work without a coordination point, but gives up any per-workload affinity

properties.value: The policy carries substantial cross-request state (a prefix-locality table per server, per-band rotation cursors, live endpoint telemetry, per-workload queues) and draws on a process-wide random source seeded from the wall clock.
properties.tradeoff: Refuses reproducibility: identical inputs can yield different endpoints, because the source is seeded from the current time and the picker shuffles before a stable sort. Bounds memory explicitly: the prefix table is capped at 31250 blocks per server with at most 256 blocks matched at 16 tokens each, inactive pods are swept every 2 minutes, idle flows reclaimed after 5 minutes, and the per-request response queue is capped at 100 chunks.

properties.value: running the same request against the same fleet twice can legitimately land on a different endpoint
properties.tradeoff: spreads tied traffic evenly and resists adversarial patterning, at the cost of being untestable by exact replay and unexplainable after the fact

properties.value: each piece of remembered state has an explicit size or age limit rather than growing with traffic
properties.tradeoff: memory is bounded under any traffic shape, but the caps are guesses that silently degrade accuracy once exceeded

properties.value: the step that gathers extra per-request signals is abandoned after a fixed budget and its failure never blocks the request
properties.tradeoff: bounds added latency and keeps the router available, but placement can silently proceed on degraded information

properties.value: not decided: spend is bounded by nothing. There is no price table, per-request cost estimate, budget or spend counter anywhere.
properties.tradeoff: Refuses any spend guarantee. The only bounded resources are queued bytes per priority band and per-endpoint utilisation thresholds; price never enters a scoring or admission decision.

properties.value: Every request opens a trace span tagged with target model and priority, logs the chosen endpoint and each plugin's verdict, and increments per-stage metrics; every refusal is returned to the caller as a typed error with a status and a human-readable cause.
properties.tradeoff: Guarantees that a refusal is visible to the caller WITH its cause (resource exhausted, timed out in queue, client disconnected, internal error) and that per-plugin latency, scheduling attempts, queue size, queued bytes and pool saturation are all exported. Refuses to surface enrichment failures: they are logged and the request proceeds on degraded information, indistinguishable to the caller from a fully informed decision.
